To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the dissociation energies of the metal-carbon bonds are in the range 2.2 to 3.8 eV, and the excitation energy of the metal is in the range 1.0 to 2.8 eV.
the dissociation energy of a metal-carbon bond is a linear function of the excitation energy of the metal, and that the slope of the line is the same for all metals.
the dissociation energies of the metal-carbon bond are 3-5 times larger for metals than they are for non-metals and that the excitation energies are 2-3 times larger.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the determination of the dissociation energies of metal carbon bonds in a series of volatile methyl compounds, the calculation of the internal energies of excitation of the metals concerned, and the correlation of these energies with other properties of the elements.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the dissociation energy of a metal-carbon bond is a function of the excitation energy of the metal, and that this excitation energy in turn is a function of a number of factors, the most important of which are the position of the element in the Periodic System and its atomic weight.
the metal-carbon bond is stronger than the metal-metal bond and the carbon-carbon bond, but weaker than the metal-halogen bond.

the metal-carbon bonds in methyls, and presumably in other organic compounds, are weaker than those of the non-metals, that the bond energies are in the main inversely proportional to the excitation energies, and that the bond energies increase with the atomic weight.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the metal-carbon bond is weaker than the non-metal-carbon bond and that the metal-carbide bond is stronger than the metal-carbon one.

the dissociation energies of metal- carbon bonds are not greatly influenced by the internal excitation energy of the metal atom, but that the excitation energy of a metal atom does affect the magnitude of the excitation energies which the metal-carbon bond possesses.

the metal-carbon bond is stronger the more the metal resembles a metal, i.e., the more it is capable of assuming a positive oxidation state, and the less it is capable of forming a stable compound with carbon monoxide.
